gist: Opens the chapter on the Mysteries: identifies the Hermetic Art with Greek Theurgy, rejects modern readings of the Mysteries as fraud or mere symbolism, insists the rites really procured Ontological Wisdom and purification of the soul, and argues that modern Mesmerism works in the same material as the ancients but without their principles, discipline or aim of purifying the Vital Spirit.

notes.point: Epigraph: the path to Deity is arduous; its first gates are bound with chains of brass; Egyptians disclosed the road by actions, and other ancient peoples knew it.
notes.voice: QUOTED: Oracle of Apollo, from Eusebius

notes.point: The Greeks borrowed the Hermetic Art with their metaphysics from Egyptians and Persians, whose temples nearly every noted philosopher visited.

The Hermetic Art or Art of Divine works was called Theurgy by the Greeks, practised at Eleusis. Inquirers dismissed the Mysteries as priestly pantomime; yet Church Fathers carried their language, disciplines and rites into Christian worship, and Clemens Alexandrinus called them "blessed".

Modern interpreters rejected: Warburton (political fraud; greater mysteries meant to nullify the lesser), Sainte Croix (astronomical), Gebelin and La Pluche (agricultural), Antiquity Unveiled (religious melancholy); even Thomas Taylor (immaterial ceremonies representing abstract truths). None credit a discovery of the Wisdom professed.

Antiquity holds philosophy, i.e. Ontological Wisdom, as the object of initiation and the rites as really efficacious to procure it. They were called Initia as the beginning of a life of reason and virtue, raising men from a brutal life and to hope of blessed immortality.

Promised only to Greater Mysteries initiates: assimilation and final contact with the identity whence we first descend. Iamblicus: Theurgists reached the Wisdom of true Being by divinely potent arts and ineffable media, not contemplation or faith. Heraclitus called these medicines of imperfect souls; they healed bodies too.

Strabo: philosophy was the Eleusinian object. Servius: Bacchic rites purified souls. The Greeks held the rites secured the states' welfare and gave moral enlightenment and purification; without them existence was a living death. Tragedians (Euripides, Sophocles) made chief felicity consist in them.
notes.voice: QUOTED: Strabo, Servius, the Greeks, Euripides, Sophocles

notes.point: Clemens: the Greater Mysteries unveiled nature; the Lord is hierophant, sealing the adept. The church hid its mysteries, especially the final apotheosis, using obscure terms only initiates grasp (Cyrillus).
A secret attached to Ethnic and Christian celebrations, distinct from ordinary worship, which never essentially changes the state of life.

Writers on Animal Magnetism suggest their Trance reveals the temple mysteries, but none rose above therapy or studied the ancient rites; with that key they would see the ancients sought far superior results.
Mesmerism relieves pain and cures, but lucidity, prevision and community of sense, will and thought led nowhere further; the science has retrograded.

Mesmerism's best effects are trifles beside the Sacred Art's Wisdom, Self-Knowledge and immortality. It has not investigated the subject-being causing its effects; sleepwalkers lack a guide and discrimination; the Universal Medium is taken in its natural state, without knowing how to improve, raise or lower it; tests only identify the same Imponderable.

The ancients worked the same material with similar instruments, but on established principles. Theurgists condemned the natural Spirit as degraded, passed its first revelations in the Lesser Mysteries, dissolved the medium further, and separated the Vital Spirit from defilements and sense-impressions obscuring the divine eye, through which, purified, all truth is perceived.
Surviving Neoplatonists (Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry, Synesius, Iamblicus) show the Spirit's disease and clarification; by lustrations the soul is liberated into a divine condition.

method.veiled: Now the Egyptians, that is the Hermetic Art, or Art of Divine works, was by the Greeks called Theurgy
method.plain: The Hermetic Art (the Egyptian 'Art of Divine works') is the same thing the Greeks called Theurgy, practised in the Mysteries at Eleusis and other temples.
method.basis: II.2 ¶3 asserts the identity directly; ¶7 calls it the ancients' Sacred Art.

also.text: if we connect it with the ancients’ Sacred Art

method.veiled: philosophy, that is to say, Ontological Wisdom, as the true object of initiation
method.plain: The goal of initiation was real knowledge of Being (Ontological Wisdom), not ceremony or allegory.
method.basis: II.2 ¶4 glosses philosophy as Ontological Wisdom; ¶5 Iamblicus: 'the Wisdom of true Being'; Strabo: philosophy the object of the Eleusinian rites.

also.text: became cognizant partakers in the Wisdom of true Being
philosophy, according to Strabo, was the object of the Eleusian rites

method.veiled: represents the rites themselves as really efficacious to procure it
method.plain: The rites actually produced the Wisdom; they were not representations of abstract truths (the view Atwood rejects in Taylor).
method.basis: II.2 ¶4 contrasts this with Taylor's 'immaterial ceremonies, representations at best of abstract philosophic truths'.

method.veiled: by certain ineffable and sublime media that Theurgists became cognizant partakers in the Wisdom of true Being
method.plain: Theurgists reached the Wisdom by effective operative means ('arts divinely potent'), not by contemplation, belief or symbolic representation. This chunk does not say what the media were.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5 states the contrast explicitly; the nature of the media is not given.

also.text: it was by arts divinely potent, and not by theoretic contemplation only or by mere doctrinal faith or representations either of reality

method.veiled: Heraclitus calls these medicines, as being the help and remedy of imperfect souls
method.plain: The theurgic media are called 'medicines' because they heal imperfect souls; they could heal the body too.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5 gives the reason for the name and adds 'they possessed a power of healing the body likewise'.

method.veiled: Initia, for they were the beginning of a life of reason and virtue
method.plain: Initiation marks the start of a new rational and virtuous life, lifting one out of an irrational, brutal life and toward hope of immortality.
method.basis: II.2 ¶4 explains the name.

method.veiled: an assimilation was induced, and final contact with the object of rational inquiry, which is that identity whence, as a principle, we make our first descent
method.plain: The final result, granted only in the Greater Mysteries, is becoming like and touching the original source from which the soul first descended.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5 defines the object as 'that identity whence ... we make our first descent'; restriction to Greater Mysteries stated in same paragraph.
method.voice: QUOTED: the Pythagoreans, Plato in Phaedo (endorsed)

also.text: to those who were initiated in the Greater Mysteries only

method.veiled: the sacred rites of Bacchus pertained to the purification of souls
method.plain: The rites worked by purifying the soul; one kind of purgation in Bacchic rites was an 'airing' of the soul. This chunk does not explain the airing.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5 Servius and the Latin (translation ours for the second phrase); ¶5 'moral enlightenment and purification of life'; ¶9 lustrations liberate the soul.

also.text: Animae aere ventilatur, quod erat in sacris Liberi purgationis genus.
celebrating orgies in the mountains with holy purifications

method.veiled: nature and all things she contains were unveiled
method.plain: In the Greater Mysteries instruction ended in a direct revelation of the whole of nature.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5: 'The doctrine of the Greater Mysteries ... related to the whole universe; here all instruction ended'.

also.text: At the light of torches the veil that covers deity and heaven falls off.

method.veiled: it is the Lord himself who is the hierophant; he sets his seal upon the adept whom he illuminates with his beams
method.plain: The true initiator is the divine itself, which marks and illuminates the initiate.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5, Clemens' words; Atwood does not gloss them.

method.veiled: except in obscure terms, in such a manner, however, as that the faithful who are initiated may comprehend, and the rest be discouraged
method.plain: The mysteries, especially the 'final apotheosis', were deliberately spoken of only in enigmas readable by initiates, to deter the uninitiated.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5 St Cyrillus, and 'the usage of the church as not to discover its mysteries to the profane'.

also.text: For by these enigmas the Dagon is overthrown

method.veiled: There was undoubtedly a secret, hanging about these celebrations, both Ethnic and Christian
method.plain: The Mysteries held a secret that, unlike ordinary worship, essentially changed the initiate's state of life.
method.basis: II.2 ¶5: ordinary worship 'might indeed be perpetuated anywhere ... without essentially, changing the state of life', implying the Mysteries do change it.

method.veiled: the Self-Knowledge and perfection of life and immortality promised
method.plain: The higher Mysteries promised Supreme Wisdom, Self-Knowledge, perfection of life and immortality.

method.veiled: suggest their Trance and its phenomena as a revelation of the temple mysteries
method.plain: Atwood treats the mesmeric trance as a possible 'key' to the temple mysteries, but only a starting point; the ancients pursued far higher results through Theurgic disciplines.
method.basis: II.2 ¶6 'with that key in hand' (referent not explicit: the Trance or inquiry into the ancient rites); ¶7 'if we connect it with the ancients’ Sacred Art'; ¶8 same material and instruments.

method.veiled: although working in the same material and with similar instruments, on the same ground, yet their practice was different
method.plain: Mesmerists and the ancient Theurgists worked on the same material with similar means; the difference lay in principles and aim.
method.basis: II.2 ¶8, continuing the comparison with Mesmerism in ¶7.

also.text: it was conducted upon established principles and with a truly philosophic as well as benevolent aim

method.veiled: the subject-being, the cause of its own effects
method.plain: The effects of Mesmerism have a cause in a 'subject-being' that mesmerists have not investigated. This chunk does not further define it.
method.basis: II.2 ¶7 rhetorical question about Mesmerism's failure to investigate it.

method.veiled: the Universal Medium
method.plain: The medium that mesmerism uses is capable of improvement, of ascending or descending, and has a 'right determination'; mesmerists take it in its natural state. ¶8 speaks of the ancients dissolving 'the medium' further (referent: see ambiguities).
method.basis: II.2 ¶7 'having no knowledge of the capabilities or means of improvement, whither it is able to ascend or descend, or what is its right determination'; ¶8 'dissolve the medium more entirely'.

also.text: identify the same Imponderable through all

method.veiled: Our sleepwalkers are little better than dreamers
method.plain: Entranced subjects left to themselves lack a guide, cannot develop their latent faculties, and cannot tell true revelations from false.
method.basis: II.2 ¶7 continues: 'without a guide, unable of themselves to educate their latent talents, or discriminate truth from falsehood in their revelations'.

also.text: repeating the same mechanical operations, and witnessing similar effects continually over and over again

method.veiled: condemn the Spirit of the natural life as degraded and incapable of true intelligence
method.plain: The spirit in its ordinary natural state is unfit for true knowledge; its first-level revelations (cf. the mesmeric revelations criticized in ¶7) are not to be valued.
method.basis: II.2 ¶8: 'nor did they therefore value the revelations of its first included sphere'.

method.veiled: passing these, as it appears, in the Lesser Mysteries, to dissolve the medium more entirely
method.plain: The Lesser Mysteries apparently covered and went beyond the first sphere of natural-spirit revelations; the work then went on to a fuller dissolution of the medium.
method.basis: II.2 ¶8 ('as it appears' is Atwood's own hedge); ¶5 restricts the final promise to the Greater Mysteries.

method.veiled: to segregate the Vital Spirit away from those defilements and imaginative impressures which, by the birth into sense, had become implanted there
method.plain: The core operation: separate the Vital Spirit from the impurities and imprinted images acquired through embodiment in the senses, which obscure intelligence.

method.veiled: that divine eye which, as Plato says, is better worth than 10,000 corporeal eyes
method.plain: An inner faculty of perception, once purified and strengthened by appropriate aids, sees the truth of all beings.
method.basis: II.2 ¶8: 'by looking through this alone, when it is purified and strengthened by appropriate aids, the truth pertaining to all beings is perceived'.

method.veiled: in what the disease of the Spirit consists, and from what cause it falsifies and is dulled
method.plain: The Spirit is in a diseased state that makes it give false and dulled results; the Neoplatonists explain this in part.
method.basis: II.2 ¶9; this chunk does not itself describe the disease.

method.veiled: how it becomes clarified and defecated, and restored to its innate simplicity
method.plain: The Spirit is cleared and purged of its dregs, returning to its original simple state; by the lustrations the soul is freed into a divine condition.

also.text: by the lustrations in the Mysteries, as they describe, the soul becomes liberated and passes into a divine condition of being

method.veiled: And the strong massy gates thro’ which we pass, In our first course, are bound with chains of brass;
method.plain: The first stage of the path is barred and hard to pass. This chunk does not explain the image.
method.basis: II.2 ¶1 epigraph only; the road was 'Disclosed by actions infinite', consistent with ¶5's emphasis on operative arts, but not explained.
method.voice: QUOTED: Oracle of Apollo, from Eusebius

also.text: Disclosed by actions infinite this road.

ambiguities.quote: Now the Egyptians, that is the Hermetic Art, or Art of Divine works, was by the Greeks called Theurgy
readings: The Egyptians' art, i.e. the Hermetic Art, was called Theurgy by the Greeks (grammar defective).
Read literally the sentence equates 'the Egyptians' with the Hermetic Art.
ambiguities.basis: Singular 'was' and the following 'practiced at Eleusis' fit the art, not the people; ¶2 says the Greeks borrowed the Art from the Egyptians.

ambiguities.quote: to dissolve the medium more entirely
readings: 'the medium' is the Universal Medium of ¶7.
'the medium' is the Spirit of the natural life / Vital Spirit named in the same sentence.
ambiguities.basis: ¶7 discusses the Universal Medium's capacity for improvement; ¶8's sentence goes on to segregate the Vital Spirit, suggesting they may be one subject.

ambiguities.quote: identify the same Imponderable through all
readings: The Imponderable is the Universal Medium named in the previous sentence.
A distinct agent identified by experiments.
ambiguities.basis: Adjacent sentences in ¶7; no explicit identity asserted.

ambiguities.quote: by certain ineffable and sublime media
readings: Operative means akin to the mesmeric agency, given ¶8 'working in the same material and with similar instruments'.
Unspecified rites whose nature this chunk withholds.
ambiguities.basis: ¶5 gives no content; ¶6–¶8 link Mesmerism to the ancients' practice.

threads.note: "We have shown in our history that the Greeks were not ignorant of the Hermetic Art" — refers to Atwood's earlier historical account.
"the Platonist and Psellus, before cited to the point" — earlier citations on the Mysteries as Initia.
"Previous, however, to more fully entering" — a fuller treatment of the Mysteries is to follow.
"besides those before named" — Neoplatonist authors previously named.
